name: Boano (Maluku)
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation exists verbatim in the cited open-access source, now, but on printed p.82, not p.83: correct the locator and register the copy consulted (grade field is blank). The source is a 1983 historical-comparative monograph whose stress statement is made for the Hoamoal subgroup as a whole (Boano is a member in Collins's tree, p.73) and exemplified with Luhu; no Boano forms with stress marks are given, so the evidence for Boano specifically is second-order. Nothing better appears to exist: Glottolog has zero descriptive references for boan1242, and Grimes & Edwards 2026 (opened, sec. 10.3.1) know only Stresemann 1927, Collins 1983 and Taguchi 1989 for Boano and say nothing about its stress. sources.citation: Collins 1983, The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Pacific Linguistics D-47, p.83, full PDF via web.archive.org copy of sealang.net
sources.quote: An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: ANU. (open PL scan; copied from)
sources.quote: "Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress." (examples Luhu vs Asilulu; p.82 bottom: "This obligatory penultimate stress rule ... seems to be the motivating force for certain vowel deletions in the antepenultimate syllable.")
sources.locator: printed p.82 (p.92); Boano placed in West Hoamoal, tree p.73, cf. p.84

sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026. The Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste: Unravelling their prehistory and classification. (Languages of the New Guinea Region 1.) Berlin: Language Science Press. (open access; text copied from)
sources.quote: None for Boano; section treats segmental historical phonology (*d/*z/*R/*l/*j reflexes, diphthongs) and notes Boano as somewhat divergent within Ambon-Seram.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1982. Linguistic research in Maluku: a report of recent field work. Oceanic Linguistics 21(1/2): 73-146.

sources.note: 74-pp fieldwork report by the same fieldworker covering the West Seram/Manipa Strait languages individually; the only likely place for Boano-specific phonological notes (our classification rests on a group-level 'all Hoamoal languages' sentence illustrated with Luhu, not Boano).
